BPM Justification: Assessing, disclosing, and mitigating sustainability impacts describes a recurring assess-review-mitigate governance cycle that can inform how organizations track process-level environmental impact, though the guideline targets product/project impact broadly rather than a specific process model.

Understanding user requirements is a standard design-phase input to any system including a process model, but as written this targets UX/interface requirements rather than process participant or activity design specifically.
This concerns integrating sustainability checks into product ideation and branding, a generic design-process practice with no specific connection to business process structure or execution.

Designing efficient, minimal-step user journeys directly parallels core BPM process design goals of eliminating unnecessary steps and gateways, even though the guideline is framed around web navigation rather than BPMN modeling.
This is a UI-behavior guideline about avoiding distracting interface elements; it affects how a human-task UI is built but has no bearing on process structure or orchestration.
Avoiding manipulative UI patterns and respecting tracking consent is a UX/ethics concern implemented at the individual task/UI level, generic to any interactive system.

Reusable, well-documented deliverables loosely echo BPM's reuse of subprocess libraries and process documentation, but the guideline targets code/design assets generally rather than process models specifically.
Purely a front-end interface consistency practice with no connection to process modeling, execution, or data.
Concerns optimizing media assets in a UI; unrelated to process orchestration or design.
A front-end animation/motion guideline with no process design implication.
A typography/font-loading performance guideline, entirely front-end and unrelated to BPM.

Notification preference management is an application-level UX concern; while process task assignments can trigger notifications, this guideline addresses generic opt-in/consent controls, not escalation or process-event design.

Explicitly promotes digital-first workflows replacing paper-based processes, a direct and common BPM digitization/redesign scenario, though it focuses on document formats rather than full process orchestration. It also explicitly addresses the documents carried through that workflow (formats, reuse, previews), a distinct process-data mechanism alongside the workflow redesign.
Early prototype validation is a generic design/UX research practice; it could inform process design but the guideline itself is about interface prototypes, not process models.

Regular auditing and testing 'in simulated and real-world scenarios' echoes process simulation and audit practices conceptually, but the guideline addresses software bug testing generically, not process model validation.
Monitoring feature usage and feedback to guide improvement is generic product analytics; it resembles process monitoring only by loose analogy.
Cross-device/browser compatibility testing is purely a front-end technical concern.
Setting performance/energy targets for content and code is a generic engineering practice at the individual asset level, not a process-level KPI-setting activity.
Pure code-size optimization technique, unrelated to process design or execution.
Front-end bundling/modularization technique with no process modeling relevance.
Refactoring to avoid code duplication is generic software engineering hygiene; only a loose analogy exists to avoiding duplicate process fragments.

Minimizing and carefully loading third-party integrations parallels minimizing calls to external service tasks in a process, though the guideline as written targets web page scripts/widgets rather than enterprise service orchestration.
A markup/code-quality standard with no process design connection.
Front-end resource loading strategy, unrelated to process orchestration.
Structured metadata improves machine readability of content generally; it only weakly touches process data exchanged between activities.
A CSS/responsive-design technique with no bearing on process design or execution.
Responsive/progressive layout adaptation is a front-end concern; 'carbon-aware' here refers to rendering choices, not process scheduling.
Code-level API/JS efficiency guidance, unrelated to process modeling or orchestration.
Keeping dependencies minimal and updated is generic software maintenance that applies equally to any worker implementation, with no process-specific angle.
Website configuration/metadata files are a purely technical web-hosting concern.
Choosing the most efficient implementation approach could apply to a service task's backing implementation, but the guideline is generic implementation-choice advice for any software component.
Using up-to-date languages/runtimes is generic technical maintenance applicable to worker implementations but not process-specific.

Minimizing/scoping database queries and applying data governance practices directly concerns how process data is stored and retrieved by service tasks, a recurring BPM data-management issue even though it is framed generically here.

Selecting low-carbon hosting/region and extending hardware lifespan directly determines where and how process orchestration engines and workers run, matching the rubric's core example of region selection.

Caching and offline support reduce network load generically; a process engine or its workers could apply caching for reference data, but this is a broad infrastructure technique, not a process-specific one.
Compressing server responses and media is a generic infrastructure/transport optimization with no distinct process design implication.
Web error-page and redirect handling is a website usability concern, unrelated to process modeling or execution.
Removing unnecessary virtualized environments is general infra hygiene; it can reduce idle process-engine or worker containers but is not specific to BPM.

'Run processes only when needed' is a direct process-execution efficiency principle (event-driven/on-demand triggering over constant polling), closely matching how BPM process instances should be triggered. The guideline also separately calls out scaling 'infrastructure efficiently', a distinct infrastructure-layer mechanism alongside the process-triggering one.
Deciding how often to refresh data is directly analogous to configuring timer/cycle events and data-sync cadence in a process model, balancing freshness needs against sustainability cost.
Routine backups are a generic IT resilience practice; process instance/history data would be included, but the guideline is not process-specific.

Carbon-aware scheduling of data processing is a core green-BPM concern -- deciding when to trigger process execution or batch jobs based on grid carbon intensity is a direct, common process-design and execution decision.
CDN use for static content delivery is a generic web-performance/infrastructure technique with little bearing on process orchestration.
Demand-matched autoscaling infrastructure is the rubric's explicit example of core BPM relevance -- orchestrated workers/process engines scaling to actual demand rather than being overprovisioned.
Retention, compression, and lifecycle policies for stored data (including logs) directly parallel BPM's need to govern process history/instance data retention over time.
Publishing organization-wide ethics/sustainability policies is broad corporate governance; it can constrain how processes are designed but is not itself a process-specific practice.
Appointing a sustainability advocate is a generic organizational role assignment; only weakly analogous to naming a process owner in BPM governance.
Sustainability training and onboarding is generic organizational HR/L&D practice with no process-model-specific angle.
Communicating environmental impact of user choices is a UX/transparency feature, generic and not process-orchestration specific.

Calculating full life-cycle environmental impact 'including those of third-party services' directly matches assessing the sustainability cost of external services invoked from a process (e.g., service tasks calling third-party APIs), informing process and vendor design decisions. Since it explicitly names third-party services as part of the assessment, it also concretely touches the worker/task layer where those external services are actually invoked.
Defining measurable sustainability goals and metrics is exactly the kind of organizational KPI work that feeds process-level dashboards and monitoring targets in BPM.
Independent verification of sustainability claims is a generic audit/compliance practice; analogous only loosely to process compliance audits.

Standards-aligned sustainability reporting over time depends on underlying process performance data and monitoring outputs, giving it a genuine, if indirect, tie to BPM analysis and reporting pipelines.
Describing how revenue supports environmental/social outcomes is business-model strategy with no process-design specificity.
A maintenance strategy with resourcing, measurement, and early failure-risk detection closely resembles ongoing process governance and monitoring for process/service health.
Maintaining continuous improvement procedures that balance changes against value and sustainability outcomes is directly the BPM optimization lifecycle phase applied to a product/process.
Documenting updates for users is generic product-change communication with no specific BPM angle.
Evaluating whether a digital product/service is even necessary parallels the BPM practice of questioning whether a process or activity is value-adding before investing in its design.

Selecting and measuring suppliers by sustainability criteria maps directly onto vendor/service-provider selection for external services invoked by a process, a concrete process-design and procurement concern.
Fair pay and employee benefits are labor/HR practices unrelated to process design or execution.

Ensuring human oversight and challenge mechanisms for automated decisions maps directly onto BPM patterns for human-in-the-loop review, escalation, and override of automated/rule-based decision tasks within a process. The guideline separately mandates involving users and staff in decision-making and providing transparency, a distinct organizational/governance mechanism (stakeholder power-sharing) alongside the process-level override pattern.
Diversity/equity/inclusion commitments are organizational culture practices with no distinct process-modeling implication.

Managing the user-data lifecycle (minimized collection, portability, deletion) is the substance of common BPM examples like GDPR erasure/consent workflows, making this a genuine process-data governance concern.

Governing responsible use of AI/automated systems, including environmental impact and workforce adaptation, is increasingly relevant as processes incorporate AI-driven service tasks or RPA, though the guideline speaks at an organizational policy level. It also concretely constrains the data and models used by those automated systems, a distinct worker/task-level mechanism (the backing implementation of AI-driven service tasks) alongside the organizational policy.
Divesting from high-carbon assets and sustainable financial partnerships is corporate finance strategy, unrelated to process design.
Corporate philanthropy and giving policy has no connection to business process design or execution.

Planning and documenting a product's shutdown and what happens to user data parallels the BPM concern of process retirement/decommissioning and disposition of process instance data. The guideline explicitly names what happens to users' data as part of shutdown planning, a distinct process-data mechanism alongside the governance decision to retire the product.
Repair, reuse, and recycling of hardware is an IT asset-lifecycle practice with no process-modeling specificity.

Defining performance/environmental/human budgets with evidence-based KPIs tracked over time is precisely the kind of organizational metric-setting that BPM monitoring dashboards and process KPIs are built on.
An open-source contribution policy is organizational strategy unrelated to process design, though it may tangentially cover open-source BPM tooling.

Tested incident-response/business-continuity plans map directly onto BPM's exception-handling constructs (error/compensation events, escalation paths) that keep processes resilient to disruption. A business continuity plan is itself an organizational governance artifact maintained and tested at the policy level, distinct from the process-level exception-handling constructs it translates into.
